# message-port.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/adapters/message-port.mdx

title: Message Port
description: Use Silgi over MessagePort — Electron, browser extensions, Web Workers.

Silgi can run over any `MessagePort`-compatible channel — Electron IPC, browser extension ports, Web Workers, iframes.

## Server side

Attach your router to a port:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { createHandler } from 'silgi/message-port'
import { appRouter } from './router'

const port = getPort() // MessagePort, Worker, chrome.runtime.Port, etc.

createHandler(appRouter, port, {
  context: () => ({
    db: getDB(),
  }),
})
```

## Client side

Connect to the same port from the other end:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { MessagePortLink } from 'silgi/message-port'
import { createClient } from 'silgi/client'
import type { AppRouter } from './router'

const port = getPort()

const client = createClient<AppRouter>({
  links: [new MessagePortLink(port)],
})

const users = await client.users.list()
```

## Electron example

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// main.ts (main process)
import { createHandler } from 'silgi/message-port'

ipcMain.handle('rpc-port', (event) => {
  const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannelMain()
  createHandler(appRouter, port1, { context: () => ({}) })
  event.senderFrame.postMessage('rpc-port', null, [port2])
})
```

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// renderer.ts (renderer process)
import { MessagePortLink } from 'silgi/message-port'
import { createClient } from 'silgi/client'

const port = await getElectronPort()
const client = createClient<AppRouter>({
  links: [new MessagePortLink(port)],
})
```

## What's next?

- [Client](/docs/client) — client configuration and links
- [Integrations](/docs/integrations) — other available integrations

# nestjs.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/adapters/nestjs.mdx

title: NestJS
description: Use Silgi as a NestJS controller — Express or Fastify under the hood.

Register Silgi as a NestJS controller. Works with both Express and Fastify adapters.

## Setup

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// rpc.controller.ts
import { Controller, All, Req, Res } from '@nestjs/common'
import { createHandler } from 'silgi/nestjs'
import { appRouter } from './rpc'

const rpcHandler = createHandler(appRouter, {
  context: (req) => ({ db: getDB(), user: req.user }),
})

@Controller('api')
export class RpcController {
  @All('*')
  async handle(@Req() req: Request, @Res() res: Response) {
    return rpcHandler(req, res)
  }
}
```

Procedures are accessible at:

```
POST /api/users/list
POST /api/users/create
```

## Context from NestJS

The context factory receives the Express/Fastify request. Access guards, pipes, and other NestJS features through the request:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
createHandler(appRouter, {
  context: (req) => ({
    user: req.user, // from NestJS AuthGuard
    ip: req.ip,
    headers: req.headers,
  }),
})
```

<Callout type='info'>
  NestJS's own dependency injection, guards, and interceptors run before the Silgi handler. You can use `@UseGuards()`,
  `@UseInterceptors()`, etc. alongside Silgi.

## What's next?

- [Express](/docs/integrations/express) — if you don't need NestJS's DI
- [Integrations](/docs/integrations) — other available integrations

# nextjs.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/adapters/nextjs.mdx

title: Next.js
description: Use Silgi with Next.js App Router — API routes with full type safety and protocol support.

Silgi integrates with Next.js App Router via catch-all API routes. Full content negotiation (JSON, MessagePack, devalue) works out of the box.

## Setup

Create a catch-all API route:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// app/api/[...path]/route.ts
import { createHandler } from 'silgi/nextjs'
import { appRouter } from '~/server/rpc'

const handler = createHandler(appRouter, {
  context: (req) => ({
    db: getDB(),
    headers: Object.fromEntries(req.headers),
  }),
})

export { handler as GET, handler as POST }
```

Procedures are accessible at:

```
POST /api/users/list
POST /api/users/create
GET  /api/health
```

## Server Actions

For server-first React apps, use [React Server Actions](/docs/integrations/react) instead of API routes:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// app/actions.ts
'use server'
import { createAction } from 'silgi/react'

export const listUsers = createAction(appRouter.users.list)
```

## Edge Runtime

The handler uses standard Fetch API — works on both Node.js and Edge runtime:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
export const runtime = 'edge'
```

<Callout type='info'>
  Silgi compiles the router once at module load time. Next.js caches module imports across requests, so the compilation
  cost is paid only once per cold start.

## Analytics and Scalar

Enable the built-in [analytics dashboard](/docs/analytics) or [Scalar API reference](/docs/scalar) directly in the adapter:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const handler = createHandler(appRouter, {
  context: (req) => ({ headers: Object.fromEntries(req.headers) }),
  analytics: {
    auth: process.env.ANALYTICS_TOKEN,
  },
  scalar: true,
})
```

- [Analytics](/docs/analytics) — built-in monitoring dashboard
- [React Server Actions](/docs/integrations/react) — `[error, data]` tuple pattern

# nitro.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/adapters/nitro.mdx

title: Nitro
description: Use Silgi with Nitro v3 — modular server entry with analytics, tracing, and typed procedures.

import { Files, Folder, File } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/files'

[Nitro](https://nitro.build) is the server engine behind Nuxt and TanStack Start. Silgi integrates with Nitro using the `serverEntry` config — Silgi becomes the server framework.

## Project structure

<Files>
  <File name='nitro.config.ts' />
  <File name='server.ts' />
  <Folder name='server/rpc' defaultOpen>
    <File name='instance.ts' />
    <File name='router.ts' />
    <Folder name='todos' defaultOpen>
      <File name='schema.ts' />
      <File name='index.ts' />
    </Folder>
    <Folder name='auth'>
      <File name='schema.ts' />
      <File name='index.ts' />
    </Folder>
  </Folder>
</Files>

## Setup

### 1. Silgi instance

```ts title="server/rpc/instance.ts"
import { silgi } from 'silgi'
import { todos } from './todos/schema'

export const s = silgi({
  context: () => ({ todos }),
})
```

### 2. Procedures with tracing

```ts twoslash title="server/rpc/todos/index.ts"
// @noErrors
import { trace } from 'silgi/analytics'
import { s } from '../instance'
import { CreateTodoSchema, TodoIdSchema, TodoListSchema, TodoSchema, OkSchema, getNextId } from './schema'

export const list = s
  .$route({ tags: ['Todos'], summary: 'List all todos' })
  .$output(TodoListSchema)
  .$resolve(async ({ ctx }) => {
    return trace(ctx, 'db.todos.findMany', () => [...ctx.todos])
  })

export const create = s
  .$input(CreateTodoSchema)
  .$output(TodoSchema)
  .$resolve(async ({ input, ctx }) => {
    const todo = { id: getNextId(), title: input.title, completed: false, createdAt: new Date().toISOString() }
    await trace(ctx, 'db.todos.insert', () => ctx.todos.push(todo))
    return todo
  })

export const toggle = s
  .$input(TodoIdSchema)
  .$output(TodoSchema)
  .$errors({ NOT_FOUND: 404 })
  .$resolve(async ({ input, ctx, fail }) => {
    const todo = await trace(ctx, 'db.todos.findById', () => ctx.todos.find((t) => t.id === input.id))
    if (!todo) return fail('NOT_FOUND')
    todo.completed = !todo.completed
    return todo
  })

export const remove = s
  .$input(TodoIdSchema)
  .$output(OkSchema)
  .$errors({ NOT_FOUND: 404 })
  .$resolve(async ({ input, ctx, fail }) => {
    const idx = ctx.todos.findIndex((t) => t.id === input.id)
    if (idx === -1) return fail('NOT_FOUND')
    ctx.todos.splice(idx, 1)
    return { ok: true }
  })
```

### 3. Router

```ts title="server/rpc/router.ts"
import * as auth from './auth'
import { s } from './instance'
import * as todos from './todos'

export const appRouter = s.router({
  auth: {
    login: auth.doLogin,
    logout: auth.doLogout,
    me: auth.me,
  },
  todos: {
    list: todos.list,
    create: todos.create,
    toggle: todos.toggle,
    remove: todos.remove,
  },
})

export type AppRouter = typeof appRouter
```

### 4. Server entry

```ts title="server.ts"
import { s } from './server/rpc/instance'
import { appRouter } from './server/rpc/router'

export default {
  fetch: s.handler(appRouter, {
    scalar: true,
    analytics: {
      auth: process.env.ANALYTICS_TOKEN,
    },
  }),
}
```

### 5. Nitro config

```ts title="nitro.config.ts"
import { defineNitroConfig } from 'nitro/config'

export default defineNitroConfig({
  compatibilityDate: '2025-01-01',
})
```

<Callout>
  Nitro detects the `fetch` method on the default export and routes all requests through it. The analytics dashboard is
  available at `/api/analytics`.

## Coexisting with existing routes

When you add Silgi to an app that already has its own routes — GraphQL endpoints, REST API routes, file-system routes — the default `fetch` export takes over **all** requests. To let unmatched routes fall through to Nitro's normal routing:

```ts twoslash title="server.ts"
// @noErrors
import { silgi } from 'silgi'

const s = silgi()
const appRouter = s.router({
  health: s.$resolve(() => ({ status: 'ok' })),
})

const silgiHandler = s.handler(appRouter)

export default {
  fetch: async (request: Request) => {
    const response = await silgiHandler(request)
    if (response.status === 404) return
    return response
  },
}
```

## What's next?

- [Nuxt](/docs/integrations/nuxt) — Silgi with Nuxt 4 (Vue pages, typed client composable)
- [Analytics](/docs/analytics) — built-in monitoring dashboard
- [Server](/docs/server) — standalone `serve()` with full protocol support

# nuxt.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/adapters/nuxt.mdx

title: Nuxt
description: Use Silgi with Nuxt 4 — modular server routes, typed client composable, analytics, and WebSocket support.

import { Tabs, Tab } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/tabs'
import { Files, Folder, File } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/files'

[Nuxt](https://nuxt.com) uses Nitro under the hood. Silgi integrates via the `serverEntry` config, giving you a modular RPC layer alongside Nuxt's file-system routing, auto-imports, and Vue pages.

## Project structure

<Files>
  <File name='nuxt.config.ts' />
  <File name='server.ts' />
  <Folder name='server/rpc' defaultOpen>
    <File name='instance.ts' />
    <File name='router.ts' />
    <File name='guards.ts' />
    <Folder name='todos' defaultOpen>
      <File name='schema.ts' />
      <File name='index.ts' />
    </Folder>
    <Folder name='auth'>
      <File name='schema.ts' />
      <File name='index.ts' />
    </Folder>
  </Folder>
  <Folder name='app'>
    <Folder name='composables'>
      <File name='useClient.ts' />
    </Folder>
    <Folder name='pages'>
      <File name='index.vue' />
      <File name='todos.vue' />
    </Folder>
  </Folder>
</Files>

## Setup

### 1. Silgi instance

```ts title="server/rpc/instance.ts"
import { silgi } from 'silgi'
import { todos } from './todos/schema'

export const s = silgi({
  context: () => ({ todos }),
})
```

### 2. Procedures

```ts title="server/rpc/todos/schema.ts"
import { z } from 'zod'

export const TodoSchema = z.object({
  id: z.number(),
  title: z.string(),
  completed: z.boolean(),
  createdAt: z.string(),
})

export const CreateTodoSchema = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200) })
export const TodoIdSchema = z.object({ id: z.number() })

export type Todo = z.infer<typeof TodoSchema>

export const todos: Todo[] = [{ id: 1, title: 'Buy groceries', completed: false, createdAt: '2026-03-20T10:00:00Z' }]
```

```ts twoslash title="server/rpc/todos/index.ts"
// @noErrors
import { trace } from 'silgi/analytics'
import { s } from '../instance'
import { CreateTodoSchema, TodoIdSchema, TodoListSchema, TodoSchema } from './schema'

export const list = s
  .$route({ tags: ['Todos'], summary: 'List all todos' })
  .$output(TodoListSchema)
  .$resolve(async ({ ctx }) => {
    return trace(ctx, 'db.todos.findMany', () => [...ctx.todos])
  })

export const create = s
  .$input(CreateTodoSchema)
  .$output(TodoSchema)
  .$resolve(async ({ input, ctx }) => {
    const todo = { id: Date.now(), title: input.title, completed: false, createdAt: new Date().toISOString() }
    ctx.todos.push(todo)
    return todo
  })
```

### 3. Router

```ts title="server/rpc/router.ts"
import * as todos from './todos'
import { s } from './instance'

export const appRouter = s.router({
  todos: {
    list: todos.list,
    create: todos.create,
  },
})

export type AppRouter = typeof appRouter
```

### 4. Server entry

```ts title="server.ts"
import { s } from './server/rpc/instance'
import { appRouter } from './server/rpc/router'

export default {
  fetch: s.handler(appRouter, {
    analytics: { auth: process.env.ANALYTICS_TOKEN },
  }),
}
```

### 5. Nuxt config

```ts title="nuxt.config.ts"
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  compatibilityDate: '2025-01-01',
})
```

<Callout>No `serverEntry` config is needed — Nuxt automatically detects `server.ts` at the project root.</Callout>

## Typed client composable

Create a composable that gives Vue components a fully typed RPC client:

```ts title="app/composables/useClient.ts"
import { createClient } from 'silgi/client'
import { createLink } from 'silgi/client/ofetch'
import type { AppRouter } from '../../server/rpc/router'

export function useClient() {
  const link = createLink({ url: '' })
  return createClient<AppRouter>(link)
}
```

Use it in any page or component:

```vue title="app/pages/todos.vue"
<script setup lang="ts">
const client = useClient()
const { data: todos } = await useAsyncData(() => client.todos.list())
</script>

<template>
  <ul>
    <li v-for="todo in todos" :key="todo.id">{{ todo.title }}</li>
  </ul>
</template>
```

## Binary protocols

Silgi supports MessagePack and Devalue codecs alongside JSON. Pass `binary` or `devalue` to the link:

```ts
export function useClient(options?: { binary?: boolean; devalue?: boolean }) {
  const link = createLink({
    url: '',
    binary: options?.binary,
    devalue: options?.devalue,
  })
  return createClient<AppRouter>(link)
}
```

<Callout type='info'>MessagePack requires `msgpackr` in `vite.optimizeDeps.include` to work in dev mode.</Callout>

## Coexisting with Nuxt routes

When Silgi handles all requests, Nuxt's own server routes and pages won't work. To let unmatched routes fall through:

```ts title="server.ts"
const silgiHandler = s.handler(appRouter)

export default {
  fetch: async (request: Request) => {
    const response = await silgiHandler(request)
    if (response.status === 404) return
    return response
  },
}
```

- [Analytics](/docs/analytics) — built-in monitoring dashboard
- [Client](/docs/client) — typed RPC client setup
- [TanStack Query](/docs/integrations/tanstack-query) — query/mutation options generation

# peer.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/adapters/peer.mdx

title: Peer-to-Peer
description: Bidirectional RPC between two Silgi instances — Electron, Web Workers, browser extensions.

Two peers that can call each other's procedures simultaneously. Uses MessagePort or any bidirectional channel.

## Setup

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { createPeer } from 'silgi/peer'

// Peer A (e.g., Electron main process)
const peerA = createPeer(mainRouter, channel.port1)

// Peer B (e.g., Electron renderer)
const peerB = createPeer(rendererRouter, channel.port2)

// A calls B's procedures
const data = await peerA.client.getRendererState()

// B calls A's procedures
const files = await peerB.client.readFiles({ dir: '/tmp' })
```

## Use cases

- **Electron**: main ↔ renderer communication with typed RPC
- **Web Workers**: main thread ↔ worker thread
- **Browser extensions**: background ↔ popup/content scripts
- **Node.js Worker Threads**: parent ↔ child

## How it works

`createPeer()` does two things on the same port:

1. **Serves** your local router (handles incoming requests)
2. **Creates** a typed client for the remote peer's router

Messages are tagged with `__type: "request"` or `__type: "response"` so they don't conflict.

## Cleanup

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
peerA.dispose() // stop listening
peerB.dispose()
```

## What's next?

- [Message Port](/docs/integrations/message-port) — one-way RPC (server + client on separate ports)
- [Integrations](/docs/integrations) — other available integrations

---

# remix.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/adapters/remix.mdx

title: Remix
description: Use Silgi with Remix action/loader routes.

[Remix](https://remix.run) uses file-based routing with `action` and `loader` exports. Silgi integrates via a catch-all splat route.

## Setup

Create a catch-all route:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// app/routes/api.$.tsx
import { createHandler } from 'silgi/remix'
import { appRouter } from '~/server/rpc'

const handler = createHandler(appRouter, {
  context: (args) => ({
    db: getDB(),
    headers: Object.fromEntries(args.request.headers),
  }),
})

export const action = handler
export const loader = handler
```

Procedures are accessible at:

```
POST /api/users/list
POST /api/users/create
GET  /api/health
```

## Context from Remix loaders

The `context` function receives the standard Remix `LoaderFunctionArgs` / `ActionFunctionArgs` object:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
createHandler(appRouter, {
  context: (args) => ({
    user: args.context.user, // from Remix server context
    params: args.params,
  }),
})
```

## Analytics and Scalar

Enable the built-in [analytics dashboard](/docs/analytics) or [Scalar API reference](/docs/scalar) directly in the adapter:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const handler = createHandler(appRouter, {
  context: (args) => ({ headers: Object.fromEntries(args.request.headers) }),
  analytics: {
    auth: process.env.ANALYTICS_TOKEN,
  },
  scalar: true,
})
```

## What's next?

- [Analytics](/docs/analytics) — built-in monitoring dashboard
- [Server](/docs/server) — standalone `serve()` as an alternative
- [Integrations](/docs/integrations) — other available integrations

```ts twoslash
import { createHandler } from 'silgi/sveltekit'
```

## Context from SvelteKit hooks

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// src/hooks.server.ts
export async function handle({ event, resolve }) {
  event.locals.user = await getUser(event.cookies.get('session'))
  return resolve(event)
}
```

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// src/routes/api/[...path]/+server.ts
const handler = createHandler(appRouter, {
  context: (event) => ({
    user: event.locals.user,
```

# ai-sdk.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/ai-sdk.mdx

title: AI SDK
description: Turn Silgi procedures into AI tools — LLMs call your API through function calling.

import { Step, Steps } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/steps'

The [Vercel AI SDK](https://sdk.vercel.ai) lets you connect LLMs to **tools** — functions the model can call when it needs data or wants to take actions. Silgi can automatically convert your procedures into AI tools, extracting JSON Schema from your Zod input schemas.

This means your existing API becomes callable by AI models with zero extra code.

## Prerequisites

You need a Silgi [router](/docs/getting-started) and the AI SDK:

```bash
npm install ai @ai-sdk/openai
```

(Or any other AI SDK provider — Anthropic, Google, etc.)

## Quick start

<Steps>
<Step>

### Convert your router to tools

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { routerToTools } from 'silgi/ai'
import { appRouter } from './router'

const tools = routerToTools(appRouter)
```

This creates one AI tool per procedure. Nested routers are flattened with underscores: `users.list` becomes `users_list`, `admin.stats` becomes `admin_stats`.

</Step>
<Step>

### Use with any model

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { generateText } from 'ai'
import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai'

const { text } = await generateText({
  model: openai('gpt-4o'),
  tools,
  prompt: 'List all users with limit 5, then create a user named Bob',
})
```

The model sees your procedures as callable functions. It reads the descriptions and parameter schemas, decides which tools to call, and Silgi executes them.

</Step>
</Steps>

## How it works

For each procedure, Silgi:

1. **Extracts a description** from `route.description` or `route.summary` in your procedure definition. Falls back to `"Call {name}"`.
2. **Converts the Zod input schema** to JSON Schema, which is the format LLMs use for function calling.
3. **Creates an AI SDK `tool`** that executes the procedure when the model calls it.

This means your existing route metadata doubles as AI tool documentation:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const listUsers = s
  .$input(z.object({ limit: z.number().optional() }))
  .$route({
    summary: 'List all registered users',
    description: 'Returns a list of users, optionally limited by count.',
  })
  .$resolve(({ input, ctx }) => ctx.db.users.findMany({ take: input.limit }))
```

The AI model sees `"List all registered users"` as the tool description and knows it can pass `{ limit: number }` as input.

## Single procedure

For more control, convert individual procedures instead of the whole router:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { procedureToTool } from 'silgi/ai'

const searchTool = procedureToTool('search', appRouter.search, {
  description: 'Search the database for items matching a query',
})

const { text } = await generateText({
  model: openai('gpt-4o'),
  tools: { search: searchTool },
  prompt: 'Find all items related to TypeScript',
})
```

The `description` option overrides anything from the procedure's route metadata.

## Filtering procedures

You probably don't want to expose every procedure to the AI. Use the `filter` option to control which ones become tools:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const tools = routerToTools(appRouter, {
  // Only expose query procedures, not mutations
  filter: (path, procedure) => procedure.type === 'query',
})
```

Or filter by path:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const tools = routerToTools(appRouter, {
  filter: (path) => !path.startsWith('admin_'),
})
```

## Custom descriptions

Override descriptions for specific tools:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const tools = routerToTools(appRouter, {
  descriptions: {
    users_list: 'Get a list of all registered users. Supports a limit parameter.',
    users_create: 'Create a new user account with a name and email.',
  },
})
```

These take priority over route metadata.

<Callout>
  Good descriptions matter. LLMs decide which tool to call based on the description. Be specific about what the tool
  does and what parameters it accepts.

## Supported input types

The Zod-to-JSON-Schema converter handles common types:

| Zod type              | JSON Schema                                          |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `z.string()`          | `{ "type": "string" }`                               |
| `z.number()`          | `{ "type": "number" }`                               |
| `z.boolean()`         | `{ "type": "boolean" }`                              |
| `z.object({...})`     | `{ "type": "object", "properties": {...} }`          |
| `z.array(z.string())` | `{ "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } }` |
| `z.enum(["a", "b"])`  | `{ "type": "string", "enum": ["a", "b"] }`           |
| `z.optional(...)`     | Marked as not required                               |

For procedures without an input schema, the tool accepts an empty object.

## What's next?

- [Getting Started](/docs/getting-started) — set up a Silgi router to convert into tools
- [Procedures](/docs/procedures) — add route metadata that becomes tool descriptions
- [Integrations](/docs/integrations) — other available integrations

---

# better-auth.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/better-auth.mdx

title: Better Auth
description: Trace Better Auth operations in silgi analytics — login flows, OAuth, session management with structured attributes.

import { Tabs, Tab } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/tabs'

The Better Auth integration traces every auth operation — sign-in, sign-up, OAuth flows, session management — into silgi analytics. Each operation appears as a span with `user.id`, `session.id`, `auth.operation`, and success/failure status. Two integration points cover both HTTP requests and programmatic API calls.

## Setup

<Tabs items={['pnpm', 'npm', 'bun']}>
  <Tab value='pnpm'>```bash pnpm add silgi better-auth ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='npm'>```bash npm install silgi better-auth ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='bun'>```bash bun add silgi better-auth ```</Tab>
</Tabs>

There are two ways to trace auth operations:

1. **`tracing()` plugin** — traces HTTP-level auth requests (sign-in forms, OAuth callbacks)
2. **`instrumentBetterAuth()`** — traces programmatic `auth.api.*` calls (server-side session fetches, background jobs)

Use one or both depending on your setup.

## Plugin setup

Add `tracing()` to your Better Auth plugins. Pass `createAuthMiddleware` from `better-auth/api` so the plugin can wrap the after-hook handler:

```ts twoslash title="auth.ts"
// @noErrors
import { betterAuth } from 'better-auth'
import { createAuthMiddleware } from 'better-auth/api'
import { tracing } from 'silgi/better-auth'

export const auth = betterAuth({
  database: { url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  plugins: [tracing({ createAuthMiddleware })],
})
```

## Handler setup

In your silgi handler, call `setRequestContext(request, ctx)` before passing the request to Better Auth. This bridges the silgi request context to the auth plugin via a GC-friendly `WeakMap` — no mutation of the `Request` object.

```ts twoslash title="server.ts"
// @noErrors
import { silgi } from 'silgi'
import { setRequestContext } from 'silgi/better-auth'
import { auth } from './auth'

const s = silgi()

const authHandler = s.$resolve(async ({ ctx, request }) => {
  setRequestContext(request, ctx)
  return auth.handler(request)
})

const appRouter = s.router({
  auth: { handler: authHandler },
})

export default { fetch: s.handler(appRouter) }
```

<Callout type='warn'>
  `setRequestContext(request, ctx)` must run before `auth.handler(request)`. Without it the plugin has no access to the
  request trace and spans are silently skipped.

<Callout>
  The legacy `(request as any).__silgiCtx = ctx` assignment still works as a fallback for existing code, but new code
  should prefer `setRequestContext` — it avoids mutating the `Request` and releases the entry automatically when the
  `Request` is GC'd.

## What gets captured

Each auth operation produces a span with these attributes:

| Attribute        | Type      | Description                                                         |
| ---------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `auth.operation` | `string`  | Operation name (`signin`, `signup`, `signout`, `get_session`, etc.) |
| `auth.method`    | `string`  | Auth method (`email`, `oauth`)                                      |
| `auth.provider`  | `string`  | OAuth provider name (`google`, `github`, etc.)                      |
| `auth.success`   | `boolean` | Whether the operation succeeded                                     |
| `user.id`        | `string`  | Authenticated user's ID                                             |
| `user.email`     | `string`  | Authenticated user's email                                          |
| `session.id`     | `string`  | Session ID                                                          |

## Operation mapping

The plugin maps Better Auth URL paths to structured span names:

| Path                   | Span name                        | Operation         |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------- |
| `/sign-up/email`       | `auth.signup.email`              | `signup`          |
| `/sign-in/email`       | `auth.signin.email`              | `signin`          |
| `/sign-out`            | `auth.signout`                   | `signout`         |
| `/get-session`         | `auth.get_session`               | `get_session`     |
| `/update-user`         | `auth.update_user`               | `update_user`     |
| `/delete-user`         | `auth.delete_user`               | `delete_user`     |
| `/change-password`     | `auth.change_password`           | `change_password` |
| `/change-email`        | `auth.change_email`              | `change_email`    |
| `/verify-email`        | `auth.verify_email`              | `verify_email`    |
| `/forget-password`     | `auth.forgot_password`           | `forgot_password` |
| `/reset-password`      | `auth.reset_password`            | `reset_password`  |
| `/list-sessions`       | `auth.list_sessions`             | `list_sessions`   |
| `/revoke-session`      | `auth.revoke_session`            | `revoke_session`  |
| `/sign-in/{provider}`  | `auth.oauth.initiate.{provider}` | `oauth_initiate`  |
| `/callback/{provider}` | `auth.oauth.callback.{provider}` | `oauth_callback`  |

Unrecognized paths fall back to `auth.{last_segment}` with operation `unknown`.

## Programmatic API tracing

For server-side calls to `auth.api.*` (session validation, background user management), use `instrumentBetterAuth` with `withCtx`:

```ts twoslash title="auth.ts"
// @noErrors
import { betterAuth } from 'better-auth'
import { instrumentBetterAuth } from 'silgi/better-auth'

export const auth = instrumentBetterAuth(
  betterAuth({
    database: { url: process.env.DATABASE_URL! },
  }),
)
```

Then wrap API calls in `withCtx`:

```ts twoslash title="server.ts"
// @noErrors
import { silgi } from 'silgi'
import { withCtx } from 'silgi/better-auth'
import { auth } from './auth'

const s = silgi()

const me = s.$resolve(async ({ ctx, request }) => {
  return withCtx(ctx, () => auth.api.getSession({ headers: request.headers }))
})
```

Programmatic spans are named `auth.api.{operation}` (e.g. `auth.api.get_session`, `auth.api.signin`). All known API methods are mapped to their operation names automatically. Unknown methods are also traced using a camelCase-to-snake_case conversion of the method name.

## Configuration

Options for the `tracing()` plugin:

| Name                   | Type       | Default     | Description                                                                       |
| ---------------------- | ---------- | ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `captureInput`         | `boolean`  | `true`      | Capture request body as span input                                                |
| `captureOutput`        | `boolean`  | `true`      | Capture response data as span output                                              |
| `createAuthMiddleware` | `function` | `undefined` | Pass `createAuthMiddleware` from `better-auth/api` to wrap the after-hook handler |

---

# broker.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/broker.mdx

title: Message Broker
description: Call procedures across services via NATS, Redis, or any message broker.

import { Tabs, Tab } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/tabs'
import { Steps, Step } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/steps'

Normally Silgi talks over HTTP. But sometimes your services need to talk to each other through a message broker like NATS or Redis. The broker adapter lets you do exactly that — same router, same client, just a different transport underneath.

## How it works

You pick a **driver** for your broker. The driver handles the messaging — Silgi handles everything else (routing, validation, errors, types).

<Mermaid chart='sequenceDiagram\n    participant A as Service A (client)\n    participant B as NATS / Redis\n    participant C as Service B (server)\n    A->>B: client.users.list()\n    B->>C: deliver request\n    C->>B: { users: [...] }\n    B->>A: deliver response' />

Every driver has two sides:

- **Server** listens for requests and sends back results
- **Client** sends requests and waits for results

The API is the same regardless of which broker you use.

## NATS

NATS is the easiest option — it has built-in request-reply, so everything just works.

<Tabs items={['pnpm', 'npm', 'bun']}>
  <Tab value='pnpm'>```bash pnpm add silgi nats ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='npm'>```bash npm install silgi nats ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='bun'>```bash bun add silgi nats ```</Tab>
</Tabs>

<Steps>
<Step>
### Connect to NATS and create a driver

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { connect } from 'nats'
import { natsBroker } from 'silgi/broker/nats'

const nc = await connect({ servers: 'localhost:4222' })
const driver = natsBroker(nc)
```

</Step>

<Step>
### Start the server

Pass your router and the driver. This is identical to how you'd use `handler()` — just over NATS instead of HTTP.

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { createBroker } from 'silgi/broker'
import { appRouter } from './router'

await createBroker(appRouter, driver, {
  context: () => ({ db: getDB() }),
})
```

</Step>

<Step>
### Call from the client

The client works exactly like the HTTP client. Same types, same autocomplete.

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { BrokerLink } from 'silgi/broker'
import { createClient } from 'silgi/client'
import type { AppRouter } from './router'

const client = createClient<AppRouter>(new BrokerLink(driver))

const users = await client.users.list({ limit: 10 })
```

</Step>
</Steps>

### Scaling with queue groups

If you run multiple server instances, pass `queue` so each request goes to only one of them:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { natsBroker } from 'silgi/broker/nats'

// all instances use the same group name — NATS load-balances automatically
const driver = natsBroker(nc, { queue: 'api-workers' })
```

## Redis

Redis works too, but it doesn't have built-in request-reply like NATS. The driver simulates it using temporary channels — you don't need to worry about the details.

<Tabs items={['pnpm', 'npm', 'bun']}>
  <Tab value='pnpm'>```bash pnpm add silgi ioredis ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='npm'>```bash npm install silgi ioredis ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='bun'>```bash bun add silgi ioredis ```</Tab>
</Tabs>

<Callout type='info'>
  Redis needs two connections — one for publishing, one for subscribing. This is a Redis limitation, not a Silgi one.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Create the driver

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import Redis from 'ioredis'
import { redisBroker, ioredisTransport } from 'silgi/broker/redis'

const redis = new Redis()
const driver = redisBroker(ioredisTransport(redis, redis.duplicate()))
```

</Step>

<Step>
### Start the server

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { createBroker } from 'silgi/broker'
import { appRouter } from './router'

await createBroker(appRouter, driver, {
  context: () => ({ db: getDB() }),
})
```

</Step>

<Step>
### Call from the client

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { BrokerLink } from 'silgi/broker'
import { createClient } from 'silgi/client'
import type { AppRouter } from './router'

const client = createClient<AppRouter>(new BrokerLink(driver))

const users = await client.users.list({ limit: 10 })
```

</Step>
</Steps>

## Using a different broker

If you use RabbitMQ, MQTT, or something else, you can write your own driver. It's just two functions:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import type { BrokerDriver } from 'silgi/broker'

function myBroker(client: MyBrokerClient): BrokerDriver {
  return {
    // Server side: listen for requests, call reply() with the result
    subscribe(subject, handler) {
      const sub = client.subscribe(subject, (msg) => {
        handler(msg.payload, (response) => client.send(msg.replyTo, response))
      })
      return () => sub.unsubscribe()
    },
    // Client side: send a request, wait for the response
    async request(subject, payload, opts) {
      return client.request(subject, payload, { timeout: opts?.timeout })
    },
  }
}
```

## Testing

Use `memoryBroker()` in your tests — it works the same way but runs in-memory, no Docker needed:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { createBroker, BrokerLink, memoryBroker } from 'silgi/broker'
import { createClient } from 'silgi/client'

const driver = memoryBroker()
await createBroker(appRouter, driver)
const client = createClient<AppRouter>(new BrokerLink(driver))

// now test as usual
const result = await client.health()
```

## What's next?

- [Client](/docs/client) — client configuration
- [Message Port](/docs/integrations/message-port) — RPC over MessagePort (Electron, Web Workers)

---

# drizzle.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/drizzle.mdx

title: Drizzle ORM
description: Trace every Drizzle ORM query in silgi analytics — zero config, automatic SQL capture.

import { Tabs, Tab } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/tabs'

Every database query is a potential bottleneck. The Drizzle integration wraps your Drizzle instance so every `select`, `insert`, `update`, and `delete` appears as a span in silgi analytics — with duration, SQL text, table name, and operation type. No manual instrumentation needed.

## Setup

Install both packages:

<Tabs items={['pnpm', 'npm', 'bun']}>
  <Tab value='pnpm'>```bash pnpm add silgi drizzle-orm ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='npm'>```bash npm install silgi drizzle-orm ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='bun'>```bash bun add silgi drizzle-orm ```</Tab>
</Tabs>

Wrap your Drizzle instance with `instrumentDrizzle`, then use `withCtx` inside procedures to connect queries to the current request trace:

```ts twoslash title="server.ts"
// @noErrors
import { silgi } from 'silgi'
import { instrumentDrizzle, withCtx } from 'silgi/drizzle'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres'
import * as schema from './schema'

const db = instrumentDrizzle(drizzle(process.env.DATABASE_URL!, { schema }), { dbName: 'myapp' })

const s = silgi()

const listUsers = s.$resolve(async ({ ctx }) => {
  return withCtx(ctx, () => db.select().from(schema.users))
})

export default { fetch: s.handler(s.router({ users: { list: listUsers } })) }
```

## What gets captured

Each query produces a span with these attributes:

| Attribute        | Type      | Description                                            |
| ---------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `db.system`      | `string`  | Database system identifier (default: `postgresql`)     |
| `db.name`        | `string`  | Logical database name (e.g. `auth`, `ecommerce`)       |
| `db.operation`   | `string`  | SQL operation (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) |
| `db.statement`   | `string`  | Full SQL text (truncated to `maxQueryTextLength`)      |
| `db.transaction` | `boolean` | `true` when the query runs inside a transaction        |
| `net.peer.name`  | `string`  | Database host                                          |
| `net.peer.port`  | `number`  | Database port                                          |

## Span naming

Spans are named using the pattern `db.{operation}.{table}`:

```
db.select.user          — SELECT from user table
db.insert.order         — INSERT into order table
db.update.product       — UPDATE on product table
db.delete.session       — DELETE from session table
db.tx.select.user       — SELECT inside a transaction
db.tx.insert.order_item — INSERT inside a transaction
```

This is more useful than generic names like `db.query` — you can immediately see which table and operation is slow in your analytics dashboard.

## Configuration

All options are optional. Pass them as the second argument to `instrumentDrizzle`:

| Name                 | Type      | Default        | Description                                           |
| -------------------- | --------- | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `dbName`             | `string`  | `undefined`    | Logical database name. Appears as `db.name` attribute |
| `dbSystem`           | `string`  | `'postgresql'` | Database system identifier                            |
| `captureQueryText`   | `boolean` | `true`         | Include SQL text in spans                             |
| `maxQueryTextLength` | `number`  | `1000`         | Truncate SQL text after this many characters          |
| `peerName`           | `string`  | `undefined`    | Database host. Appears as `net.peer.name`             |
| `peerPort`           | `number`  | `undefined`    | Database port. Appears as `net.peer.port`             |

## Multiple databases

Instrument each database separately with a distinct `dbName`:

```ts twoslash title="db.ts"
// @noErrors
import { instrumentDrizzle } from 'silgi/drizzle'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres'

const authDb = instrumentDrizzle(drizzle(process.env.AUTH_DATABASE_URL!), {
  dbName: 'auth',
  peerName: 'db.example.com',
  peerPort: 5432,
})

const ecommerceDb = instrumentDrizzle(drizzle(process.env.ECOMMERCE_DATABASE_URL!), {
  dbName: 'ecommerce',
  peerName: 'db.example.com',
  peerPort: 5432,
})
```

In your analytics, spans from each database are distinguished by the `db.name` attribute.

## Transactions

Transaction queries are automatically detected. They get a `db.tx.` prefix in the span name and the `db.transaction: true` attribute:

```ts twoslash title="server.ts"
// @noErrors
import { withCtx } from 'silgi/drizzle'

const createOrder = s.$resolve(async ({ ctx, input }) => {
  return withCtx(ctx, () =>
    db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      // span: db.tx.insert.order
      const [order] = await tx.insert(schema.orders).values(input).returning()
      // span: db.tx.insert.order_item
      await tx.insert(schema.orderItems).values(input.items.map((item) => ({ ...item, orderId: order.id })))
      return order
    }),
  )
})
```

## Security

By default, the full SQL text is captured in spans. If your queries contain sensitive data (PII, tokens, secrets), disable SQL capture in production:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { instrumentDrizzle } from 'silgi/drizzle'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres'

const db = instrumentDrizzle(drizzle(process.env.DATABASE_URL!), {
  dbName: 'myapp',
  captureQueryText: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production',
})
```

You still get span names, durations, and operation types — just not the raw SQL.

<Callout type='warn'>
  `withCtx` is required. Without it, queries execute normally but are invisible to silgi analytics. Always wrap your database calls inside `withCtx(ctx, () => ...)` in your procedures.

---

# hey-api.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/hey-api.mdx

title: Hey API
description: Convert Hey API generated OpenAPI clients into Silgi-compatible clients.

import { Tabs, Tab } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/tabs'
import { Step, Steps } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/steps'

Convert a [Hey API](https://heyapi.dev/) generated client into a Silgi client to use it with the full Silgi ecosystem — TanStack Query, Pinia Colada, and other integrations.

<Callout type='warn'>
  [Hey API](https://heyapi.dev/) is still in an unstable stage. This integration may introduce breaking changes in the
  future.

## Setup

<Steps>
<Step>

### Generate a Hey API client

Use `@hey-api/openapi-ts` to generate a typed client from your OpenAPI spec:

```bash
npx @hey-api/openapi-ts \
  -i https://api.example.com/api/openapi.json \
  -o src/client
```

This outputs the generated SDK into the `src/client` directory.

<Callout type='info'>For more information on Hey API, see the [official documentation](https://heyapi.dev/).</Callout>

</Step>
<Step>

### Convert to a Silgi client

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { toClient } from 'silgi/hey-api'
import * as sdk from './client/sdk.gen'

export const client = toClient(sdk)
```

The `client` now behaves like any standard Silgi client — you can use it with [TanStack Query](/docs/libraries/tanstack-query), [Pinia Colada](/docs/libraries/pinia-colada), or call procedures directly.

</Step>
<Step>

### Use the client

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// Direct calls
const { body } = await client.listPlanets()
console.log(body) // Planet[]

// With query params
const { body: planet } = await client.getPlanet({
  path: { planetId: 'earth' },
})

// With request body
const { body: newPlanet } = await client.createPlanet({
  body: { name: 'Mars' },
})
```

Each call returns `{ body, request, response }` where:

| Property   | Type       | Description                           |
| ---------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `body`     | `T`        | The parsed response data              |
| `request`  | `Request`  | The original `Request` object         |
| `response` | `Response` | The raw `Response` for headers/status |

</Step>
</Steps>

## With TanStack Query

Combine with `createQueryUtils` for full query/mutation support:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { toClient } from 'silgi/hey-api'
import { createQueryUtils } from 'silgi/tanstack-query'
import * as sdk from './client/sdk.gen'

const client = toClient(sdk)
const utils = createQueryUtils(client)

// Now use with useQuery, useMutation, etc.
const options = utils.listPlanets.queryOptions({ input: {} })
```

## With Pinia Colada

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { toClient } from 'silgi/hey-api'
import { createSilgiVueColadaUtils } from 'silgi/pinia-colada'
import * as sdk from './client/sdk.gen'

const client = toClient(sdk)
const utils = createSilgiVueColadaUtils(client)
```

## Error handling

Internally, Silgi passes `throwOnError: true` to the Hey API client. If the original Hey API client throws an error, it is forwarded as-is without modification.

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
try {
  const { body } = await client.getPlanet({ path: { planetId: 'unknown' } })
} catch (error) {
  // Error from Hey API — same format as the original SDK
  console.error(error)
}
```

## Abort signals

Abort signals are supported from both the input and the client options:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const controller = new AbortController()

// From input
const result = await client.listPlanets({
  signal: controller.signal,
})

// From client options
const result2 = await client.listPlanets(
  {},
  {
    signal: controller.signal,
  },
)

// Either signal aborting will cancel the request
controller.abort()
```

## What's next?

- [Client](/docs/client) — learn about Silgi clients
- [TanStack Query](/docs/libraries/tanstack-query) — use the converted client with TanStack Query
- [Pinia Colada](/docs/libraries/pinia-colada) — use the converted client with Pinia Colada
- [OpenAPI Client](/docs/libraries/openapi-client) — alternative: consume OpenAPI specs directly with `OpenAPILink`

---

# openapi-client.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/openapi-client.mdx

title: OpenAPI Client
description: Consume any OpenAPI endpoint as a typed Silgi client.

Use `OpenAPILink` to consume any OpenAPI-described API through the Silgi client interface. Bring your own spec — Silgi maps operations to procedure calls.

## Setup

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { OpenAPILink } from 'silgi/client/openapi'
import { createClient } from 'silgi/client'
import type { PetStore } from './petstore.types' // generated types

const client = createClient<PetStore>({
  links: [
    new OpenAPILink({
      url: 'https://petstore.example.com',
      spec: import('./petstore.json'),
    }),
  ],
})

const pets = await client.pets.list()
const pet = await client.pets.get({ id: '1' })
```

## Inline spec

Pass the spec object directly if you already have it:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import spec from './petstore.json'

new OpenAPILink({
  url: 'https://petstore.example.com',
  spec,
})
```

## Custom headers

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
new OpenAPILink({
  url: 'https://api.example.com',
  spec: import('./spec.json'),
  headers: () => ({
    Authorization: `Bearer ${getToken()}`,
  }),
})
```

## What's next?

- [Client](/docs/client) — client configuration and links
- [Integrations](/docs/integrations) — other available integrations

---

# pinia-colada.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/pinia-colada.mdx

title: Pinia Colada
description: Generate type-safe queryOptions, mutationOptions, and cache keys for Vue with Pinia Colada.

import { Tabs, Tab } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/tabs'
import { Step, Steps } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/steps'

[Pinia Colada](https://pinia-colada.esm.dev/) is a smart data-fetching layer for Vue built on top of Pinia. Silgi provides `createColadaUtils`, a utility that generates type-safe `queryOptions` and `mutationOptions` from your client — with full Vue reactivity support.

## Prerequisites

You need a Silgi [client](/docs/client) set up. The Pinia Colada integration wraps this client.

<Tabs items={['pnpm', 'npm', 'bun']}>
  <Tab value='pnpm'>```bash pnpm add @pinia/colada pinia vue ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='npm'>```bash npm install @pinia/colada pinia vue ```</Tab>
  <Tab value='bun'>```bash bun add @pinia/colada pinia vue ```</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Setup

<Steps>
<Step>

### Create colada utils

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { createColadaUtils } from 'silgi/pinia-colada'
import { client } from './client' // your Silgi client

const utils = createColadaUtils(client)
```

The `utils` object mirrors your client's structure. If your client has `client.users.list`, then `utils.users.list` gives you query/mutation helpers for that procedure.

</Step>
<Step>

### Use in components

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useQuery } from '@pinia/colada'

const { data, status } = useQuery(
  utils.users.list.queryOptions({
    input: { limit: 10 },
  }),
)
</script>

<template>
  <p v-if="status === 'loading'">Loading...</p>
  <ul v-else>
    <li v-for="user in data" :key="user.id">{{ user.name }}</li>
  </ul>
</template>
```

</Step>
</Steps>

## Queries

`queryOptions` returns everything `useQuery` needs — a reactive computed key and the fetch function:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const options = utils.users.list.queryOptions({
  input: { limit: 10 },
})

// options contains:
// - key: computed(() => [["users", "list"], { type: "query", input: { limit: 10 } }])
// - query: ({ signal }) => client.users.list({ limit: 10 }, { signal })
```

### Reactive inputs

Both `input` and `context` accept Vue reactive values — `ref`, `computed`, or getter functions:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

const limit = ref(10)

const options = utils.users.list.queryOptions({
  input: computed(() => ({ limit: limit.value })),
})
```

When the reactive value changes, the query key updates automatically, which triggers a refetch.

## Mutations

`mutationOptions` returns everything `useMutation` needs:

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { useMutation, useQueryCache } from '@pinia/colada'

const queryCache = useQueryCache()

const { mutate, isLoading } = useMutation({
  ...utils.users.create.mutationOptions(),
  onSuccess: () => {
    queryCache.invalidateQueries({
      key: utils.users.key(),
    })
  },
})
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="mutate({ name: 'Alice' })" :disabled="isLoading">
    {{ isLoading ? 'Creating...' : 'Create User' }}
  </button>
</template>
```

## Cache invalidation

Every level of the utils tree has a `key()` method for generating cache keys:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { useQueryCache } from '@pinia/colada'

const queryCache = useQueryCache()

// Invalidate all queries under "users"
queryCache.invalidateQueries({
  key: utils.users.key(),
})

// Invalidate a specific query with specific input
queryCache.invalidateQueries({
  key: utils.users.list.key({ type: 'query', input: { limit: 10 } }),
})

// Invalidate everything
queryCache.invalidateQueries({
  key: utils.key(),
})
```

## Direct calls

Each procedure util has a `call` property that is the original client function:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const users = await utils.users.list.call({ limit: 10 })
```

## Available methods

Each procedure-level util provides:

| Method                   | Returns                            | Description                    |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `queryOptions(opts?)`    | `{ key: ComputedRef, query, ... }` | Full options for `useQuery`    |
| `mutationOptions(opts?)` | `{ key: fn, mutation, ... }`       | Full options for `useMutation` |
| `call(input, opts?)`     | `Promise<TOutput>`                 | Direct procedure call          |

Each router-level util provides:

| Method       | Returns    | Description                      |
| ------------ | ---------- | -------------------------------- |
| `key(opts?)` | `EntryKey` | Key prefix for bulk invalidation |

<Callout type='info'>
  Input and context parameters accept `MaybeRefOrGetter` — meaning you can pass plain values, `ref()`, `computed()`, or
  getter functions. The query key is a `computed` that updates reactively.

## What's next?

- [Client](/docs/client) — set up the Silgi client that powers the colada utils
- [TanStack Query](/docs/libraries/tanstack-query) — if you prefer TanStack Query over Pinia Colada
- [Typed Errors](/docs/errors) — handle errors from your queries and mutations

---

# react.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/react.mdx

title: React Server Actions
description: Call Silgi procedures as React Server Actions — type-safe [error, data] tuples instead of try/catch.

React Server Actions let you call server-side code directly from React components. Silgi wraps your procedures as actions that return `[error, data]` tuples instead of throwing, making error handling straightforward in your UI code.

This works with **Next.js** (App Router) and **TanStack Start**.

## Prerequisites

You need a Silgi router defined on the server. If you haven't set one up yet, see the [Getting Started](/docs/getting-started) guide.

## createAction

Wraps a single procedure as a server action. Returns `[error, data]` instead of throwing.

Define the action in a file with `"use server"`:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// app/actions.ts
'use server'
import { createAction } from 'silgi/react'
import { appRouter } from '../router'

export const listUsers = createAction(appRouter.users.list)
export const createUser = createAction(appRouter.users.create)
```

Use it in a component:

```tsx
// app/page.tsx
import { listUsers } from './actions'

export default async function Page() {
  const [error, users] = await listUsers({ limit: 10 })

  if (error) {
    return <p>Error: {error.message}</p>
  }

  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map((u) => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}
```

### The return type

Every action returns a tuple: `[error, data]`.

- On success: `[null, data]` — `error` is `null`, `data` is the procedure's return value
- On failure: `[error, undefined]` — `error` has `code`, `status`, `message`, and optionally `data`

This pattern avoids try/catch in your components and makes error states explicit.

## createActions

Converts an entire router into actions at once. The result mirrors your router structure:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
'use server'
import { createActions } from 'silgi/react'
import { appRouter } from '../router'

export const actions = createActions(appRouter)
```

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// In a component or server function
const [err, users] = await actions.users.list({ limit: 10 })
const [err2, user] = await actions.users.create({ name: 'Alice' })
```

This is convenient when you have many procedures and don't want to export each one individually.

## createFormAction

For HTML `<form>` submissions, `createFormAction` accepts `FormData` and converts it into the input object your procedure expects:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// app/actions.ts
'use server'
import { createFormAction } from 'silgi/react'

export const submitUser = createFormAction(appRouter.users.create)
```

```tsx
<form action={submitUser}>
  <input name='name' required />
  <input name='email' type='email' required />
  <button type='submit'>Create User</button>
</form>
```

### Nested form data

Bracket notation in field names is automatically parsed into nested objects:

```html
<input name="user[name]" value="Alice" /> <input name="user[email]" value="alice@example.com" />
```

Becomes:

```json
{ "user": { "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com" } }
```

Array indices work too: `items[0]`, `items[1]`, etc.

### Custom parsing

If the default FormData parser doesn't match your needs, provide your own:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const submitUser = createFormAction(appRouter.users.create, {
  parseFormData: (formData) => ({
    name: formData.get('name'),
    email: formData.get('email'),
  }),
})
```

## Framework errors

Silgi automatically detects and rethrows framework-specific errors:

- **Next.js** `redirect()` and `notFound()` (errors with `NEXT_` digest)
- **TanStack Router** navigation errors (`isNotFound: true`)
- **Response** objects (used for redirects)

These errors pass through untouched — they won't be caught as `[error, data]` tuples.

<Callout>
  This means `redirect("/login")` inside a procedure works as expected in Next.js. The redirect happens, and the action
  doesn't return an error tuple.

## useServerAction

A React hook that wraps a server action with loading and error state:

```tsx
import { useServerAction } from 'silgi/react'

function CreateUserButton() {
  const { execute, data, error, isPending, reset } = useServerAction(createUser)

  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => execute({ name: 'Alice' })} disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? 'Creating...' : 'Create User'}
      </button>
      {error && <p>Error: {error.message}</p>}
      {data && <p>Created: {data.name}</p>}
    </div>
  )
}
```

`execute()` returns the same `[error, data]` tuple as the action itself, so you can also handle results inline.

## useOptimisticServerAction

Like `useServerAction`, but applies an optimistic update immediately while the server call is in flight:

```tsx
import { useOptimisticServerAction } from 'silgi/react'

function UserName({ user }) {
  const { execute, displayData, isPending } = useOptimisticServerAction(updateUser, {
    optimistic: (input) => ({ ...user, ...input }),
  })

  return (
    <div>
      <span>{displayData?.name ?? user.name}</span>
      <button onClick={() => execute({ name: 'Bob' })}>Rename</button>
    </div>
  )
}
```

- `displayData` shows the optimistic value while pending, then switches to the confirmed server response.
- If the call fails, the optimistic value is rolled back automatically.

## What's next?

- [Getting Started](/docs/getting-started) — set up a Silgi router
- [Typed Errors](/docs/errors) — how error maps and `fail()` work, and how they appear in the `error` tuple
- [TanStack Query](/docs/integrations/tanstack-query) — client-side data fetching with caching, as an alternative

---

# tanstack-query.mdx

Source: https://github.com/productdevbook/silgi/blob/main/docs/content/docs/libraries/tanstack-query.mdx

title: TanStack Query
description: Generate type-safe queryOptions, mutationOptions, and cache keys from your Silgi client.

import { Step, Steps } from 'fumadocs-ui/components/steps'

[TanStack Query](https://tanstack.com/query) is the most popular data-fetching library for React, Vue, Solid, and Svelte. Silgi provides `createQueryUtils`, a utility that generates type-safe `queryOptions` and `mutationOptions` from your client — so you don't have to write query keys or fetch functions by hand.

## Prerequisites

You need a Silgi [client](/docs/client) set up. The TanStack Query integration wraps this client.

```bash
npm install @tanstack/react-query
```

(Or `@tanstack/vue-query`, `@tanstack/solid-query`, `@tanstack/svelte-query` — the API is the same.)

## Setup

<Steps>
<Step>

### Create query utils

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
import { createQueryUtils } from 'silgi/tanstack-query'
import { client } from './client' // your Silgi client

const utils = createQueryUtils(client)
```

The `utils` object mirrors your client's structure. If your client has `client.users.list`, then `utils.users.list` gives you query/mutation helpers for that procedure.

</Step>
<Step>

### Use in components

```tsx
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query'

function UserList() {
  const { data, isLoading } = useQuery(utils.users.list.queryOptions({ input: { limit: 10 } }))

  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading...</p>
  return (
    <ul>
      {data?.map((u) => (
        <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}
```

</Step>
</Steps>

## Queries

`queryOptions` returns everything `useQuery` needs — the query key, the fetch function, and any options you pass:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const options = utils.users.list.queryOptions({
  input: { limit: 10 },
  staleTime: 5000, // data is fresh for 5 seconds
  gcTime: 60_000, // garbage collect after 1 minute
  refetchInterval: 30_000, // refetch every 30 seconds
  enabled: isLoggedIn, // only fetch when logged in
})

// options contains:
// - queryKey: [["users", "list"], { type: "query", input: { limit: 10 } }]
// - queryFn: ({ signal }) => client.users.list({ limit: 10 }, { signal })
// - staleTime, gcTime, etc.
```

Use with `useQuery`:

```tsx
const { data } = useQuery(utils.users.list.queryOptions({ input: { limit: 10 } }))
```

Or prefetch on the server:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
await queryClient.prefetchQuery(utils.users.list.queryOptions({ input: { limit: 10 } }))
```

## Mutations

`mutationOptions` returns everything `useMutation` needs:

```tsx
import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query'

function CreateUser() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient()

  const { mutate, isPending } = useMutation(
    utils.users.create.mutationOptions({
      onSuccess: () => {
        // Invalidate the user list so it refetches
        queryClient.invalidateQueries({
          queryKey: utils.users.key(),
        })
      },
    }),
  )

  return (
    <button onClick={() => mutate({ name: 'Alice' })} disabled={isPending}>
      {isPending ? 'Creating...' : 'Create User'}
    </button>
  )
}
```

## Cache invalidation

Every level of the utils tree has a `key()` method for generating cache keys:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
// Invalidate all queries under "users" (list, create, etc.)
queryClient.invalidateQueries({
  queryKey: utils.users.key(),
})

// Invalidate a specific query with specific input
queryClient.invalidateQueries({
  queryKey: utils.users.list.queryKey({ limit: 10 }),
})

// Invalidate everything in the entire app
queryClient.invalidateQueries({
  queryKey: utils.key(),
})
```

The key structure is `[path, { type, input }]`, which means TanStack Query's prefix matching works naturally. Invalidating `utils.users.key()` clears both `users.list` and `users.create` queries.

## Direct calls

If you need to call a procedure outside of React (in a loader, a utility function, etc.), each procedure util has a `call` method:

```ts twoslash
// @noErrors
const users = await utils.users.list.call({ limit: 10 }, { signal: controller.signal })
```

This is the same as calling the client directly, but it's convenient when you're already working with the utils.

## Available methods

Each procedure-level util provides:

| Method                   | Returns                            | Description                         |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `queryOptions(opts)`     | `{ queryKey, queryFn, ... }`       | Full options for `useQuery`         |
| `infiniteOptions(opts)`  | `{ queryKey, queryFn, ... }`       | Full options for `useInfiniteQuery` |
| `mutationOptions(opts?)` | `{ mutationKey, mutationFn, ... }` | Full options for `useMutation`      |
| `queryKey(input?)`       | `[path, { type, input }]`          | Query key for cache operations      |
| `mutationKey()`          | `[path, { type }]`                 | Mutation key for cache operations   |
| `call(input, opts?)`     | `Promise<TOutput>`                 | Direct procedure call               |

Each router-level util provides:

| Method        | Returns            | Description                      |
| ------------- | ------------------ | -------------------------------- |
| `key(input?)` | `[path, options?]` | Key prefix for bulk invalidation |

<Callout type='info'>
  This works with `@tanstack/react-query`, `@tanstack/vue-query`, `@tanstack/solid-query`, and `@tanstack/svelte-query`.
  Same API, same types, different framework bindings.

## Infinite queries

Use `infiniteOptions` for paginated data. It works like `queryOptions` but returns everything `useInfiniteQuery` needs:

```tsx
import { useInfiniteQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query'

function UserList() {
  const { data, fetchNextPage, hasNextPage } = useInfiniteQuery(
    utils.users.list.infiniteOptions({
      input: (pageParam) => ({ cursor: pageParam, limit: 10 }),
      initialPageParam: 0,
      getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.nextCursor,
    }),
  )

  return (
    <>
      {data?.pages
        .flatMap((p) => p.items)
        .map((u) => (
          <p key={u.id}>{u.name}</p>
        ))}
      {hasNextPage && <button onClick={() => fetchNextPage()}>Load more</button>}
    </>
  )
}
```

The `input` option is a function that receives the current page parameter and returns the procedure input. The query key includes the base input so cache invalidation works the same way as regular queries.

## skipToken

Use `skipToken` to conditionally disable a query. This is the type-safe alternative to `enabled: false` — it tells both TanStack Query and TypeScript that the query should not run:

```tsx
import { skipToken } from 'silgi/tanstack-query'
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query'

function UserProfile({ userId }: { userId: string | null }) {
  // Query is disabled until userId is available
  const { data } = useQuery(
    utils.users.get.queryOptions({
      input: userId ? { id: userId } : skipToken,
    }),
  )

  return data ? <p>{data.name}</p> : <p>Select a user</p>
}
```

When `input` is `skipToken`, the query key is still generated (for prefetching later) but `queryFn` is never called.

## Streamed queries

For subscription-like data that accumulates over time, `streamedOptions` collects all events into an array:

```tsx
function EventLog() {
  const { data: events } = useQuery(
    utils.stream.updates.streamedOptions({
      input: {},
    }),
  )

  return (
    <ul>
      {events?.map((e, i) => (
        <li key={i}>{JSON.stringify(e)}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  )
}
```

Each SSE event is appended to the array. The query resolves when the stream ends.

## Live queries

`liveOptions` refetches at an interval — the latest result replaces the previous. Useful for dashboards and status pages:

```tsx
function ServerStatus() {
  const { data } = useQuery(
    utils.health.liveOptions({
      input: undefined,
      refetchInterval: 5000, // poll every 5 seconds
    }),
  )

  return <p>Uptime: {data?.uptime}s</p>
}
```

## What's next?

- [Client](/docs/client) — set up the Silgi client that powers the query utils
- [React Server Actions](/docs/integrations/react) — an alternative for server-first React apps
- [Typed Errors](/docs/errors) — handle errors from your queries and mutations
